topics.h1: The Passive: All Tenses and Passive Infinitive
intro: The passive is **be + past participle**. To make any tense passive, put **be** in that tense: *The house **is being painted**. The report **has been finished**. The results **will be announced** tomorrow.*
For the basics, see [The Passive: Present and Past Simple](/blog/grammar/passive-present-past/).

rows: I felt like I **was being watched**.
The tickets **had been sold** before we arrived.
You **will be met** at the airport.
am / is / are going to **be** + past participle
The old cinema **is going to be closed**.
This form **must be signed**. The work **can be done** online.
The letter **should have been sent** yesterday.

blocks.md: Passives of the perfect continuous tenses (*has been being built*) are possible but very rare. Use another structure instead.

items: **to be** + past participle: *I want **to be told** the truth. The house needs **to be cleaned**.*
**being** + past participle: *She hates **being interrupted**. I don't like **being photographed**.*

blocks.md: *Need* + -ing can also have a passive meaning: *The car **needs washing**.* (= needs to be washed)

With *give, send, offer, show, tell* and *teach*, either object can become the subject. Starting with the person is more common: *They gave **me** a prize.* → ***I was given** a prize.* / *A prize **was given** to me.*

sections.h2: When to use the passive, and get + past participle

items: To focus on the action or the thing affected, not the person who did it: *The suspect **has been arrested**.*
In formal, scientific and news writing: *The samples **were analysed** in a laboratory.*

blocks.md: In informal English, **get** + past participle is common for things that happen to us, especially bad things: *He **got fired**. Our car **got stolen**.*

intro: We use **have something done** when we arrange for another person to do something for us, usually a service: *I **had my hair cut** yesterday.* (A hairdresser cut it.)
**Get something done** means the same and is more informal: *I need to **get my car fixed**.*

sections.h2: Form: have / get + object + past participle

rows: I **have my car serviced** every year.

blocks.md: Word order matters: the object goes **before** the past participle. *I had **my hair** cut* = someone cut it for me. *I had cut my hair* = past perfect: I cut it myself.
We also use *have something done* for unpleasant things that happen to us, often done by someone we don't know: *She **had her bag stolen** on the train. They **had** their flight **cancelled**.*

intro: A **non-defining relative clause** adds **extra information** about someone or something we have already identified. We put it between **commas**, and the sentence still makes sense without it: *My sister, **who lives in Dublin**, is a nurse.*

rows: *My sister **who lives in Dublin** is a nurse.* (I have more than one sister.)
*My sister, **who lives in Dublin**, is a nurse.* (I have one sister, and she lives in Dublin.)
an object pronoun can be left out
the pronoun can never be left out

blocks.md: For the basics, see [Defining Relative Clauses](/blog/grammar/defining-relative-clauses/).

rows: Mr Lee, **who** teaches us maths, is retiring.
The Eiffel Tower, **which** was completed in 1889, is in Paris.
Anna, **whose** brother is a pilot, travels a lot.
Toronto, **where** I grew up, is a big city.
In 2020, **when** the pandemic started, we worked from home.
The director, **whom** I met last year, was very kind.

blocks.md: Don't use **that** in non-defining clauses: *My car, **which** is old, still works.* (not *My car, that is old, …*)
*Which* can refer to the **whole previous clause**: *He passed all his exams, **which** surprised everyone.* (not *what surprised everyone*)

sections.h2: All of whom, some of which

blocks.md: After a quantifier, use **of whom** (people) or **of which** (things): *I have three brothers, **all of whom** live abroad. She wrote two novels, **one of which** became a film.*
Non-defining clauses are more common in writing than in conversation.

items.text: My grandmother, **who** is 90, still swims every day.
The film, **which** lasted three hours, was fantastic.
We stayed in Lisbon, **where** my cousin lives.
Mark, **whose** wife is a chef, loves cooking too.
I lost my phone, **which** was really annoying.
Our new teacher, **who** comes from Australia, is very funny.
The museum, **which** opened last year, is free on Sundays.
In July, **when** most people go on holiday, the city is quiet.
I invited ten people, **most of whom** came.
She got the job, **which** was great news.

intro: **Mixed conditionals** combine two different times. Both the condition and the result are imagined, but one is in the past and the other is in the present.
*If I **had taken** that job, I **would be** rich now.* (past condition → present result) *If I **were** taller, I **would have joined** the basketball team.* (present condition → past result)

blocks.md: **if + past perfect, would + base verb**, often with *now*: *If you **had listened** to me, you **wouldn't be** in this mess now.* (You didn't listen, so you're in a mess now.)
**if + past simple, would have + past participle**: *If I **spoke** French, I **would have understood** the film.* (I don't speak French, so I didn't understand the film.)
The present condition is usually a general fact or a permanent situation: *If she **weren't** so shy, she **would have asked** him.* *If I were* is more formal; *If I was* is common in speech.

rows: *If I had money, I'd buy a car.*
*If I'd had money, I'd have bought a car.*
*If I'd saved money, I'd have a car now.*
*If I were rich, I'd have bought that car.*

blocks.md: *Could* and *might* also work in the result: *If he had trained harder, he **might be** a professional now.*
Review the basics: [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Third Conditional](/blog/grammar/third-conditional/).

If he **had trained** harder, he **might be** a professional now.

intro: Besides *if*, English has other words to introduce conditions. **Unless** means *if … not*: *I won't go **unless** you come too.*
**Provided (that)** and **as long as** mean *only if*: *You can borrow my car **as long as** you drive carefully.*

blocks.md: *Unless* = *if not*. The verb after *unless* is positive: *We'll be late **unless** we leave now.* = *We'll be late **if** we **don't** leave now.*
Don't add a negative after *unless* when you mean *if not*: *unless you **hurry*** (not *unless you don't hurry*).

sections.h2: Provided, providing, as long as, on condition that

blocks.md: These all mean *only if* (a strong condition): *I'll lend you the money **provided (that)** you pay me back next week. You can stay out late **as long as** you text me. They agreed **on condition that** we kept it secret.* *Providing (that)* is also possible.
Like *if*, these words use the present simple for the future: *as long as you **are** home by ten* (not *will be*).

*In case* = because something **might** happen (a precaution). It isn't the same as *if*: *Take an umbrella **in case** it rains.* (Take it now, because it might rain.) *Take an umbrella **if** it rains.* (Take it only when it's raining.)

sections.h2: Even if, suppose and what if

items: **Even if** = it doesn't matter whether: *I'll go **even if** it rains.*
**Suppose / supposing** and **what if** introduce imaginary situations: ***Suppose** you won the lottery, what would you do? **What if** we miss the train?*

intro: We use **wish** and **if only** to talk about situations we want to be different. The verb after *wish* moves one step back in time: *I **wish** I **had** more time.* (I don't have enough time now.)
*If only* means the same as *I wish*, but it's stronger and more emotional.

rows: the present (you're not happy with it)
*I wish I **knew** the answer. I wish it **wasn't raining**.*
something annoying that you want to change

blocks.md: After *wish*, **were** is often used for all persons, especially in formal English: *I wish I **were** taller.* *I wish I **was** taller* is also correct, especially in speech.
For ability, use **could**: *I wish I **could** swim.*
Use *wish + would* to complain about other people's behaviour or a situation, and to show impatience: *I wish the neighbours **would** be quieter. I wish it **would** stop raining.*
We don't normally say *I wish I would…*. Use *I wish I could…* instead: *I wish I **could** come.*
*If only* uses the same tenses as *wish*: ***If only** I **had listened** to you! **If only** I **had** more money.*

Use **hope** for things that are possible: *I **hope** you **pass** your exam.* Use **wish** for things that are unreal or impossible: *I **wish** I **were** on holiday.* For good wishes, use *wish* + person + noun: *I **wish** you **a happy birthday**.*

topics.h1: Modals of Deduction in the Past (must have, can't have)
intro: To make guesses (deductions) about the **past**, use **modal + have + past participle**: *The ground is wet. It **must have rained** last night. She **might have missed** the bus. He **can't have seen** us; he didn't say hello.*

rows: You **must have been** tired after the flight.
They **might have taken** the wrong road.
**might not / may not have** + past participle
it's possible that it didn't happen
She **may not have heard** the phone.
I'm almost sure it didn't happen
He **can't have finished** already. He only started ten minutes ago.

blocks.md: In American English, **must not have** is also used for negative deductions: *He must not have heard me.*
For an action in progress, use **modal + have been + -ing**: *She **must have been sleeping** when you called.*

*Could have* + past participle can be a past possibility (*The keys **could have fallen** out of your bag*) or something that was possible but didn't happen (*You **could have called** me!* = you were able to, but you didn't). More: [Should Have, Could Have, Needn't Have](/blog/grammar/should-have-could-have-neednt-have/).
For present deductions, see [Modals of Deduction: Must, Might, Can't](/blog/grammar/modals-of-deduction-present/).
In speech, *must have* sounds like *must-uv* and *might have* like *might-uv*. In writing, always write **have**, never *of*: *It **must have** been difficult.* (not *must of*)

topics.h1: Should Have, Could Have, Needn't Have
intro: We use **modal + have + past participle** to talk about the past in different ways: what was a good idea but didn't happen (*should have*), what was possible but didn't happen (*could have*), and what happened but wasn't necessary (*needn't have*).

sections.h2: Should have and shouldn't have: regrets and criticism

blocks.md: *should have + past participle* = it was the right thing to do, but it didn't happen: *I **should have studied** harder.* (I didn't.) *shouldn't have + past participle* = it happened, but it was a mistake: *You **shouldn't have said** that.*
**Ought to have** means the same as *should have* and is a little more formal: *She **ought to have told** us.*
*could have + past participle* = it was possible, but it didn't happen: *We **could have gone** to the beach, but we stayed at home.* We also use it to criticise: *You **could have told** me!*
*couldn't have + past participle* = it was impossible: *I **couldn't have done** it without you.*

sections.h2: Needn't have or didn't need to?

rows: you did it, but it wasn't necessary
I **needn't have cooked** so much. Nobody was hungry.
it wasn't necessary (often you didn't do it)
I **didn't need to cook**, so I relaxed.

blocks.md: *Needn't have* is mainly British. American English usually says *didn't need to* or *didn't have to*: *I didn't have to cook so much.*

*would have + past participle* describes what you were willing to do, or an imagined past: *I **would have helped** you, but you didn't ask.* See [Third Conditional](/blog/grammar/third-conditional/).

topics.h1: Used To, Would, Be Used To and Get Used To
intro: These four forms look similar but mean different things:

***used to** + verb* = a past habit or state (*I **used to live** in Rome*), ***would** + verb* = a repeated past action (*We **would play** outside every day*), ***be used to** + -ing* = something is normal for you (*I**'m used to getting up** early*), ***get used to** + -ing* = something becomes normal for you (*I**'m getting used to living** alone*).

rows: past habit or state, not true now
I **used to smoke**, but I stopped.
Every summer, we **would go** to the lake.
it's normal, not strange or difficult
She**'s used to working** at night.
You'll soon **get used to** the cold.

blocks.md: For repeated **actions** in the past, you can use *used to* or *would*: *When I was a child, my grandmother **used to / would** tell me stories.*
For past **states** (*be, have, live, like, know*), use only *used to*: *I **used to have** long hair* (not *I would have long hair*).
Questions and negatives: ***Did** you **use to** play football? I **didn't use to** like vegetables.* (no -d after *did*)
See the full guide: [Used To for Past Habits](/blog/grammar/used-to/).

sections.h2: Be used to and get used to

blocks.md: Here, *to* is a **preposition**, so it's followed by a noun or **-ing**, not the base verb: *I'm used to **driving** on the right* (not *used to drive*).
*Get used to* can be in any tense: *It took me months to **get used to** it. I'm **getting used to** it. I'll never **get used to** it. I've **got used to** it.*

intro: The **future continuous** (*will be + -ing*) describes an action **in progress** at a time in the future: *This time tomorrow, I**'ll be flying** to Rome.*
The **future perfect** (*will have + past participle*) describes an action **completed before** a time in the future: *By 6 p.m., I**'ll have finished** the report.*

rows: By June, I**'ll have been living** here for five years.

blocks.md: Negatives: *I **won't be working**. She **won't have finished**.* Questions: ***Will** you **be using** the car? **Will** they **have arrived** by 8?*

items: An action in progress at a future time: *Don't call at 8. I**'ll be putting** the kids to bed.*
Something that will happen as part of the normal plan: *I**'ll be seeing** Tom at work tomorrow, so I can give him the message.*
Polite questions about someone's plans: ***Will** you **be using** the car tonight?* (more polite than *Will you use…?*)

blocks.md: Use it for something that will be **finished before** a future time, often with ***by*** (= not later than) or ***by the time***: *By 2030, scientists **will have found** a cure, I hope. By the time you wake up, we**'ll have left**.*
Use the **future perfect continuous** to say **how long** an action will have continued at a future time: *By the end of the month, she**'ll have been working** here for 20 years.*
After *by the time, when, before* and *until*, use a **present** tense for the future: *By the time you **get** home* (not *will get*). See [Future Time Clauses](/blog/grammar/future-time-clauses/).

topics.h1: Verbs That Change Meaning: -ing or To-Infinitive
intro: Most verbs take either -ing or to-infinitive. But a few verbs can take **both**, with a **different meaning**: *I **stopped smoking*** (I don't smoke now) vs *I **stopped to smoke*** (I stopped what I was doing in order to smoke).

rows: a memory of something you did before

make an effort (it may be difficult)

intro: Instead of *say* and *tell*, we often use a **reporting verb** that shows the speaker's purpose: *'I'll help you,' he said. → He **offered to help** me.*
Each reporting verb has its own **pattern**: to-infinitive, object + to-infinitive, -ing, preposition + -ing, or a *that* clause.

intro: A **phrasal verb** is a verb + a particle (*up, off, out, after…*): *turn off, look after, give up.*

Where the object goes depends on the type of phrasal verb. The most important rule: with **separable** phrasal verbs, a **pronoun** always goes **in the middle**: *Turn **it** off* (not *Turn off it*).

intro: **So** and **such** make an adjective or noun stronger: *It's **so** cold! It's **such a** cold day!*
With **that**, they show a result: *It was **so** cold **that** we stayed inside.* **So that** shows a purpose: *I left early **so that** I wouldn't miss the bus.*

rows: The film was **so** boring. She speaks **so** quickly.
They're **such** kind people. It was **such** bad weather.

blocks.md: In formal English, you may see *so* + adjective + *a* + noun: *It was **so difficult a** question that nobody could answer.* (= such a difficult question)
*The coffee was **so** hot **that** I couldn't drink it. It was **such** a long journey **that** we stopped twice.* In speech, *that* is often left out: *I was so tired I fell asleep.*

*So that* + subject + verb (often *can, could, will, would*) shows **why** someone does something: *Speak louder **so that** everyone **can** hear you. I wrote it down **so that** I **wouldn't** forget.*
Compare: *to* + verb has the same meaning when the subject is the same: *I left early **to** catch the bus.* See [Infinitive of Purpose](/blog/grammar/infinitive-of-purpose/).

topics.summary: One step further back in the past: When I arrived, the film had started.
intro: We use the **past perfect** (*had* + past participle) for something that happened **before** another moment in the past: *When I arrived, the film **had** already **started**.*
It takes you one step further back than the past simple. If you need to review the past simple first, see [Past Simple](/blog/grammar/past-simple/).

points.title: Form and main use: something earlier in the past
points.summary: had + past participle for an action before another past moment.

rows: Had she called? – No, she hadn't.

blocks.md: *Had* is the same for every person: *I had, you had, she had, they had.* Use the **past participle**: *gone, eaten, seen, been* (not *went, ate, saw*). See the list of irregular verbs on [Past Simple](/blog/grammar/past-simple/).
Think of two past moments. The past perfect is the **earlier** one: *I couldn't get in* (past) *because I **had lost** my keys* (earlier).
In speech, *had* is often **'d**: *I'd forgotten. They'd gone.* Be careful: *'d* can also mean *would* (*I'd like*). If a past participle follows, it's *had*.

examples.text: I couldn't get in because I **had lost** my keys.
She was tired because she **had worked** all night.
I **hadn't seen** the film, so I didn't know the ending.
**Had** you **been** to Asia before that trip?
The streets were wet. It**'d rained** in the night.

mistakes.wrong: I had went to bed early.
mistakes.right: I had gone to bed early.

mistakes.wrong: Had you ate before you came?
mistakes.right: Had you eaten before you came?

mistakes.wrong: She was tired because she had work all day.
mistakes.right: She was tired because she had worked all day.

points.title: Past simple or past perfect? The order of events
points.summary: Past simple for events in order; past perfect for an event that happened earlier than the one you're talking about.

blocks.md: The tense changes the **order** of events:

items: *When I arrived, the film **started**.* = I arrived, then the film started.
*When I arrived, the film **had started**.* = The film started first, then I arrived.

blocks.md: When you tell events **in the order they happened**, use the past simple. Don't use the past perfect for every past action: *I **woke up**, **had** a shower and **left** the house.*

examples.text: When we got to the station, the train **had left**.
When we got to the station, the train **left**.
When I got home, someone **had eaten** my cake.
I **got up**, **made** breakfast and **went** for a run.
I didn't know the way because I **hadn't been** there before.

mistakes.wrong: I had woken up, had had breakfast and had left.
mistakes.right: I woke up, had breakfast and left.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the film has started.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, the film had started.
mistakes.why: Earlier than a past moment: past perfect.

points.title: By the time, already, just, never … before
points.summary: by the time + past simple, then past perfect; already, just, never … before with the past perfect.

rows: *By the time we arrived, the concert **had finished**.*
*He **had just sat** down when the phone rang.*
*When she moved to Canada, she **had never seen** snow.*
***Had** you **ever** tried sushi before that night?*

blocks.md: *Already, just, never* and *ever* go between *had* and the past participle: *had **already** left, had **just** sat, had **never** seen.*

examples.text: By the time we got there, everyone **had gone** home.
She **had already ordered** when I arrived.
I**'d just got** into bed when the alarm went off.
He was nervous because he **had never flown** before.
By the time I finished my degree, my parents **had moved** to Canada.

mistakes.wrong: By the time we got there, the shop closed.
mistakes.right: By the time we got there, the shop had closed.
mistakes.why: By the time + earlier event: past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: She had left already when I called.
mistakes.right: She had already left when I called.
mistakes.why: Already goes between had and the participle.

points.title: Present perfect or past perfect?
points.summary: have done = before now; had done = before a moment in the past.

rows: *Until I moved to Canada, I**'d** never **seen** snow.*

blocks.md: The present perfect connects the past to **now**. The past perfect connects an earlier past to **a moment in the past**.

examples.text: I can't come out. I **haven't finished** my homework.
I couldn't go out because I **hadn't finished** my homework.
Last summer I visited Rome. I**'d** never **been** there before.
When I met him, he **had been** in the army for ten years.

mistakes.wrong: Before I came to Canada, I have never seen snow.
mistakes.right: Before I came to Canada, I had never seen snow.
mistakes.why: Before a past moment: past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: I'm not hungry. I'd already eaten.
mistakes.right: I'm not hungry. I've already eaten.

points.title: It was the first time I'd…; states up to a past moment
points.summary: It was the first time / the best … I'd ever + past perfect; state verbs up to a past moment use the past perfect simple.

blocks.md: After *It was the first / second / third time…* and after superlatives (*the best, the worst…*) in the past, use the past perfect: *It was the first time I**'d been** on a plane. It was the best meal we**'d** ever **had**.*

To say **how long** a state continued up to a past moment, use the past perfect simple with state verbs: *They **had known** each other for years when they got married.* (not *had been knowing*). For actions, the past perfect continuous is common: *She **had been working** there for ten years when she left.*

examples.text: It was the first time she**'d been** on a plane.
That was the third time he**'d lost** his phone that month.
It was the most beautiful place I**'d** ever **seen**.
We **had known** each other for years before we started working together.
I**'d had** the car for only a month when it broke down.

mistakes.wrong: It was the first time I've been abroad.
mistakes.right: It was the first time I'd been abroad.
mistakes.why: It was the first time + past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: We had been knowing each other for ten years.
mistakes.right: We had known each other for ten years.
mistakes.why: Know is a state: past perfect simple.

points.title: When the past perfect is optional
points.summary: If the order is already clear (after, as soon as, before) the past simple is also fine; once the earlier time is set, you can continue in the past simple.

blocks.md: When a time word like *after, as soon as* or *before* already makes the order clear, the past simple is also correct and the meaning doesn't change: *After she **had finished** / **finished** work, she went home.*

When you have **set up** an earlier time with the past perfect, you don't have to keep using it. You can continue in the past simple: *I sold my old guitar last week. I**'d had** it since I was fifteen, and I **played** it almost every day.*

But keep the past perfect when the past simple would change the order: *When I got home, my son **had cooked** dinner* (it was ready) vs *When I got home, my son **cooked** dinner* (he started after I arrived).

examples.text: After the guests **had gone** / **went**, we cleaned up.
As soon as I**'d sent** / **sent** the message, I regretted it.
She asked about the salary before she **accepted** the job.
We**'d lived** in that flat for years. We **loved** it, but it was too small.
When the police arrived, the thief **had escaped**.

mistakes.wrong: After we have eaten, we went for a walk.
mistakes.right: After we had eaten (or After we ate), we went for a walk.
mistakes.why: A past sequence: past perfect or past simple, not present perfect.

points.title: Past perfect in reported speech and thoughts
points.summary: A present perfect becomes past perfect when reported in the past; a past simple can become past perfect or stay the same.

blocks.md: When we report words or thoughts in the past, a **present perfect** usually becomes **past perfect**: *'I've met him before.' → I was sure I**'d met** him before.*
A **past simple** can become past perfect, but it can also stay in the past simple, especially when the time is clear: *'I lost my keys.' → She said she **had lost** / **lost** her keys.*
If the situation is still true now, you can also keep the present perfect: *He told me he**'s** never **been** to Asia.* See [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/).

examples.text: 'I've finished.' → She said she **had finished**.
'We haven't decided yet.' → They said they **hadn't decided** yet.
'I lost my phone.' → He said he **had lost** / **lost** his phone.
I realised I**'d left** my umbrella on the bus.
Police said twenty people **had been** / **were** injured.

mistakes.wrong: I was sure that I have met him before.
mistakes.right: I was sure that I had met him before.
mistakes.why: Reported in the past: present perfect → past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: She said she hasn't finish yet.
mistakes.right: She said she hadn't finished yet.
mistakes.why: Past perfect, with the past participle finished.

points.title: Plans that didn't happen: I had hoped to…
points.summary: had hoped / meant / intended / planned / wanted to = a plan or wish that didn't happen.

blocks.md: Use *had* + *hoped, meant, intended, planned, wanted, expected* + to-infinitive for a plan or wish that **didn't happen**: *I **had hoped** to finish by Friday, but my computer broke.*

The past simple and the continuous forms are also used with a similar meaning: *I **hoped** / **was hoping** / **had been hoping** to see you.* The past perfect makes it clearest that it didn't happen.

examples.text: We**'d hoped** to visit the museum, but it was closed.
I**'d meant** to call you, but I forgot.
She **had intended** to stay a week, but she left after two days.
They **had planned** to retire at 60, but they're still working.
I **was hoping** to see you at the party.

mistakes.wrong: I had hope to finish today, but I couldn't.
mistakes.right: I had hoped to finish today, but I couldn't.

mistakes.wrong: We had wanted visit you.
mistakes.right: We had wanted to visit you.

topics.summary: Verbs for states, not actions: I know (not I'm knowing), and when the continuous is possible.
intro: **Stative verbs** (state verbs) describe states, not actions: thoughts, feelings, senses, possession and existence.
We don't normally use them in continuous tenses: *I **know** the answer.* (not *I'm knowing*) *She **wants** a new phone.* (not *She's wanting*)

points.title: Verbs we don't use in the continuous
points.summary: know, want, like, need, understand, believe, belong… use the simple form, even for now.

rows: know, believe, understand, remember, forget, mean, realise, recognise
like, love, hate, prefer, want, need

blocks.md: Use the simple form **even when you mean now**: *I'm hungry. I **want** something to eat.* (not *I'm wanting*) *Do you **understand** what I mean?*
*Have* for possession is a state: *I **have** a car.* But *have* in phrases like *have lunch, have a shower, have fun* is an action, so the continuous is fine: *We**'re having** lunch.*

examples.text: I **don't understand** this question.
This bag **belongs** to my sister.
Do you **remember** her name?
How much **does** this jacket **cost**?
We**'re having** dinner at the moment.

mistakes.wrong: I'm knowing the answer.
mistakes.right: I know the answer.

mistakes.wrong: This book is belonging to me.
mistakes.right: This book belongs to me.

mistakes.wrong: I'm having a car.
mistakes.right: I have a car.

points.title: Verbs with two meanings: think, have, see, taste
points.summary: Some verbs are states with one meaning and actions with another; only the action meaning can be continuous.

rows: *She**'s having** lunch / a shower / a good time.*

blocks.md: With *feel* (= how your body or mood is), both forms are fine: *I **feel** tired. / I**'m feeling** tired.* But *feel* = think is a state: *I **feel** you're right.*

examples.text: I**'m thinking** of moving to Montreal.
What **do** you **think** of my new haircut?
We**'re having** a great time.
This coffee **tastes** a bit strange.
Look! The cat **is looking** at the bird.

mistakes.wrong: I'm thinking this is a good idea.
mistakes.right: I think this is a good idea.

mistakes.wrong: What do you think about? You look worried.
mistakes.right: What are you thinking about? You look worried.

mistakes.wrong: This soup is tasting delicious.
mistakes.right: This soup tastes delicious.
mistakes.why: Taste = the flavour it has: a state.

points.title: He's being rude: be in the continuous, and states in perfect tenses
points.summary: is being + adjective = behaviour right now; state verbs stay simple in perfect tenses (I've known, not I've been knowing).

blocks.md: *Be* is normally a state: *He **is** rude* = that's his character. But *be* + adjective in the continuous describes **behaviour at the moment**: *He**'s being** rude* = he is behaving rudely now (maybe that's not normal for him).
We only do this with adjectives about behaviour: *silly, rude, kind, careful, patient, difficult, quiet.* Not with things you can't control: *He's tall* (not *He's being tall*).

The same rule applies to **perfect continuous** tenses: use the perfect simple with state verbs: *I**'ve known** him for years.* (not *I've been knowing*) *They **had owned** the house for twenty years.* (not *had been owning*)

examples.text: You**'re being** very quiet today. Is everything OK?
Stop it! You**'re being** silly.
She**'s** a very patient person.
I**'ve known** Sam since primary school.
We **had** only **had** the car for a month when it broke down.

mistakes.wrong: I've been knowing her for years.
mistakes.right: I've known her for years.
mistakes.why: Know is a state: perfect simple.

mistakes.wrong: He's being tall for his age.
mistakes.right: He's tall for his age.
mistakes.why: Being + adjective is only for behaviour.

points.title: State verbs in the continuous for emphasis or change
points.summary: Informally, some state verbs take the continuous to stress a temporary feeling or a gradual change: We're loving it, I'm regretting it.

blocks.md: With some state verbs, the continuous is possible to stress that a situation is **temporary or around now**: *The kids **are loving** their new school.* *You**'re looking** great these days.* This is common in informal English.

With verbs of **mental states** (*regret, realise, understand, find*), the continuous can show a feeling that is **growing or new**: *I**'m regretting** my decision more every day. I**'m** slowly **understanding** how the system works.* *Consider* (= think about carefully) is usually continuous: *He**'s considering** a move to Vancouver.*

Some verbs are still very rarely continuous, even informally: *believe, doubt, own, belong, consist of, know.* In exams and formal writing, use the simple form with state verbs unless you have a clear reason not to.

examples.text: We**'re loving** our new flat!
You**'re looking** great these days.
I**'m regretting** that I said yes.
He**'s considering** early retirement.
We**'re hoping** to finish by Friday.

mistakes.wrong: I'm believing you now.
mistakes.right: I believe you now.

mistakes.wrong: This box is consisting of three parts.
mistakes.right: This box consists of three parts.
